topic: German and local (Münster) infrastructure for using hospital data
summary: Germany has built a large national infrastructure for structured hospital data: the research data portal counts more than 27 million persons at 41 sites, while only about 550,000 have recorded consent. RACOON connects imaging at all university hospitals and is being extended from 2026 to 2029, but its structured findings come from templates filled in by people. In Münster, MeDIC offers ORBIS extracts and a study module that can search fields and free text but no PDF documents. Hospitals such as Bonn, Magdeburg and Leipzig run language models on their own hardware; we found no university chat service that permits patient data. Evidence from Bonn and Essen shows that source-bound tasks work best and that results on real documents are lower than on synthetic ones.

findings.claim: UKM's study module in ORBIS searches structured fields and free text every night, but it cannot search PDF documents.
findings.detail: The module puts matching patients on a work list for study recruitment and has supported more than 80 studies at UKM. The page is undated, so the limit should be confirmed with MeDIC before it is shown.
findings.quote: An automatic search for information in PDF-documents is not possible.
findings.source: MeDIC, University of Münster, Study module
findings.talk_use: Local proof that documents are out of reach for today's queries; lead-in to document-to-data methods.

findings.claim: Researchers at UKM can request ORBIS data through MeDIC and the IT department and receive it as a print or Excel sheet.
findings.detail: Queries select patients by diagnosis, demographics or lab results. Results are anonymised or pseudonymised after a data protection check. The form 'Datenauszug beantragen' is in the IT section of the UKM intranet.
findings.quote: as a print or excel worksheet
findings.source: MeDIC, University of Münster, ORBIS Data extraction
findings.talk_use: Practical slide for doctoral candidates: where to ask for data.

findings.claim: In Münster a Use and Access Committee decides on applications to use patient data; Münster is a HiGHmed site.
findings.detail: The committee assesses organisational, legal, ethical and scientific aspects. MeDIC states that data usually stays in house and is evaluated by trained staff.
findings.source: MeDIC, University of Münster, Use and Access Committee
findings.talk_use: Answer to 'how do I get access to data in Münster?'.

findings.claim: Münster's MeDIC coordinates KI-AIM2, which connects an open-source anonymisation tool to hospital systems and extends it to physicians' letters.
findings.detail: Partners include Dedalus (DH Healthcare), BIH/Charité, DFKI and TMF. The tool is Cinnamon, the interface HL7 FHIR. No results published on the page.
findings.source: MeDIC, University of Münster, Research projects
findings.talk_use: Shows that the ORBIS vendor and Münster already work together on free text.

findings.claim: UKM is piloting an AI tool for doctors' letters and keeps patient data in house, according to its CIO.
findings.detail: Interview in the regional chamber of commerce magazine. It also names AI in caries detection, skin cancer screening and radiology as partly established, and several petabytes of patient data.
findings.source: IHK Nord Westfalen, UKM geht neue Wege
findings.talk_use: Local context for why methods must run on site.

findings.claim: The University of Münster's UniGPT allows information up to class V3 in local models, only public information (V1) in external models, and forbids V4.
findings.detail: UniGPT belongs to the university, not to UKM. The pages read do not name patient data; its class is defined in an internal handbook that could not be opened.
findings.number: V3 local, V1 external, V4 never
findings.quote: Informationen, die als streng vertraulich (V4) klassifiziert worden sind, dürfen nicht durch Nutzer*innen verarbeitet werden.
findings.source: University of Münster, UniGPT terms of use
findings.talk_use: Answer to 'may I paste a report into UniGPT?': no permission for patient data found; check class and ask data protection.

findings.claim: At Düsseldorf University, entering personal data into KI:connect is prohibited, even though some models run on servers in North Rhine-Westphalia.
findings.detail: Mistral Small 4 119B and GPT OSS 120B run entirely in NRW. The page says models that allow personal data are still a long way off. This is the rule at HHU; other universities set their own.
findings.quote: it is currently prohibited to enter personal data
findings.source: HHU Düsseldorf, HeiCAD, KI:connect
findings.talk_use: Shows that local hosting alone does not permit patient data.

findings.claim: The GWDG Chat AI privacy notice does not address health data; self-hosted models do not store content, external models pass it on.
findings.detail: Requests to self-hosted models are not stored permanently. Requests to external models are forwarded including personal information. The German version is binding.
findings.source: GWDG, Chat AI data privacy notice
findings.talk_use: Q&A on academic chat services.

findings.claim: RACOON has a network node at every German university hospital, connected to a central environment for structured reporting, annotation and AI.
findings.detail: Infrastructure of the Netzwerk Universitätsmedizin, started in the COVID-19 pandemic. The project page states that class IIb medical device requirements are met, which permits routine use for image diagnosis and analysis.
findings.source: Netzwerk Universitätsmedizin, RACOON
findings.talk_use: One-sentence introduction of RACOON.

findings.claim: RACOON and the pathology project NATON renew and extend the infrastructure from 2026 to 2029 at 39 university hospitals.
findings.detail: Financed by the federal special fund for infrastructure and climate neutrality. Essen receives 10.8 million euros and hosts RACOON-CENTRAL with GPU systems. Total and Münster share not found.
findings.source: University of Duisburg-Essen, Faculty of Medicine, news
findings.talk_use: Very recent news: imaging and pathology on one platform.

findings.claim: RACOON use cases in the third NUM phase (2025 to 2030) plan cohorts of about 12,000 (PAIN) and 30,000 patients (COMPARE).
findings.detail: Others are MARDER (liver MRI) and INCLUDED (childhood leukaemia, up to 33 hospitals). Figures are planned sizes from one site's overview page.
findings.source: Hannover Medical School, NUM third funding phase
findings.talk_use: Scale of current RACOON projects.

findings.claim: The template that RACOON started from had 67 items and needed more time than routine reading.
findings.detail: Proof of concept with 283 patients from 8 European centres on mint Lesion. Authors state that completeness depended on the reader and on information radiologists do not see directly.
findings.source: Salg et al., A reporting and analysis framework for structured evaluation of COVID-19 clinical and imaging data, npj Digital Medicine
findings.talk_use: Why structured data by hand does not scale: every item costs reading time.

findings.claim: Building federated learning across six RACOON hospitals worked, but the main hurdles were staff, inconsistent annotation, contracts and hospital networks.
findings.detail: 666 chest CTs collected, 582 usable. Federated models beat local ones; adding sites did not always help. Tools: mint Lesion, SATORI, ImFusion Labels, Kaapana. Münster was not among the six sites.
findings.source: Bujotzek et al., Real-world federated learning in radiology, JAMIA 32(1):193-205
findings.talk_use: Data definitions come before algorithms.

findings.claim: Structured RACOON chest CT reports could be turned into visual fingerprints that differed between 15 disease groups.
findings.detail: Single-centre retrospective study, 359 patients, RECO phase 1 template. Frequencies alone overlapped between groups; adding location and severity separated them better. The evaluation was visual.
findings.source: Bachl et al., CT Fingerprinting of Pulmonary Diseases, RoFo
findings.talk_use: Example of what becomes possible once reports are structured.

findings.claim: UKM radiologists co-authored a national RACOON study that linked CT muscle density with COVID-19 mortality in 1,379 patients.
findings.detail: Two authors list the Clinic for Radiology, University Hospital of Münster. The link held in male, not in female patients.
findings.source: Bucher et al., Academic Radiology
findings.talk_use: Public evidence for UKM's role in RACOON.

findings.claim: Germany's research data portal reports more than 27 million persons at 41 sites, but only about 550,000 with recorded consent.
findings.detail: Slide of the MII Symposium, March 2026. Also 3 billion lab values, 350 million diagnoses, 8 million radiology reports and about 140 project applications. The TMF annual report gives 21 million for the same month; heise reports 450,000 people who provided data.
findings.number: 27 million persons; 550,000 consents; 8 million radiology reports
findings.source: Overton (TMF), Aktueller Stand des FDPG, MII Symposium 2026
findings.talk_use: Big number slide: huge volume; people with consent are about 2 percent (own calculation).

findings.claim: Even with a national core data set, a multi-hospital study found significant differences in data quality and in how standards were implemented.
findings.detail: Technical report of the HELP study using data integration centres. Scripts and extraction needed several rounds with local experts. The study still showed that distributed analysis is feasible.
findings.source: Palm et al., HELP Study, JMIR Medical Informatics 13:e68171
findings.talk_use: Standards help but do not remove the need for local checks.

findings.claim: Germany's shareable clinical text corpus GeMTeX has more than 15,000 documents from six university hospitals.
findings.detail: 20 million tokens as of February 2026, consent-based, de-identified, annotation with SNOMED CT in progress. Access on request under controlled conditions.
findings.source: Hofenbitzer et al., The German Medical Text Corpus: Early 2026 Update, CMLC 2026
findings.talk_use: Contrast with billions of structured lab values: shareable text is scarce.

findings.claim: University Hospital Bonn runs an open language model on one on-premise server, approved for unanonymised patient data.
findings.detail: 8 A100 GPUs, DeepSeek-R1 671B, offered to over 10,000 employees. One-week pilot with 22 radiologists. Tasks tied to a source text were rated best; free conclusion writing produced the most critical errors. About three quarters of the preprint was read.
findings.source: Nowak et al., Secure On-Premise Deployment of Open-Weights LLMs in Radiology, arXiv 2604.22768
findings.talk_use: Best German example; supports the chain of proof: source-bound tasks work better.

findings.claim: In Magdeburg, 44 percent of surveyed users of an on-premise model reported saving at least 30 minutes a week, and 37 percent criticised answer quality.
findings.detail: 91 complete answers from 322 registered users; one H100, Llama 3.2 90B. Self-reported, likely early adopters. Cost estimate about 150 euros per million tokens versus 10 to 15 in the cloud.
findings.number: 44% save 30+ min/week; 37.4% criticise quality; about 10x cloud cost
findings.source: Grünig et al., JMIR AI
findings.talk_use: Balanced evidence on benefit and price of local models.

findings.claim: One open model on one GPU turned 96.5 percent of 2.19 million archived radiology reports into structured reports.
findings.detail: gpt-oss-120B with 150 templates, developed at one centre, tested at a second. Optimal template in 74.4 percent; residents left 88.7 percent of 24,638 fields unchanged; unsupported content flagged in 1.0 percent of radiography and 1.5 percent of CT reports; template accuracy for multi-region reports 54.1 percent. Preprint.
findings.source: Puttkammer et al., Autonomous Structuring of Radiology Reports, arXiv 2610.04541
findings.talk_use: Archive scale is feasible on one GPU, and errors show why each field still needs its source.

findings.claim: Essen's FHIR platform holds over 2 billion data objects on more than 1.4 million patients and exposed missing diabetes codes.
findings.detail: In 2022 data, 13,887 of 35,494 patients with sugar measurements had abnormal values; 44.2 percent of those had a coded diagnosis. Single hospital, retrospective. Abstract plus passages of the full text were read.
findings.source: Brehmer et al., JMIR 26:e55148
findings.talk_use: Example of a question that only structured data can answer.

findings.claim: An Essen model that extracts FHIR data from discharge letters scored up to 0.99 on synthetic letters but clearly lower on real ones.
findings.detail: On 30 real letters, physicians judged 78.9 percent of diagnoses, 93.0 percent of medications and 61.3 percent of procedures correct at case level.
findings.source: Eryılmaz et al., JMIR, 10.2196/92413
findings.talk_use: Counter-evidence: test on real documents and keep the link to the source.

findings.claim: Under section 6 GDNG, a hospital may reuse its own care data for research, but must pseudonymise it and may not pass it on without another legal basis.
findings.detail: Purposes are quality assurance, research and statistics. Anonymise as soon as possible, delete after at most 30 years, inform the public. Not legal advice.
findings.source: Gesundheitsdatennutzungsgesetz, § 6
findings.talk_use: Legal one-liner in Q&A.

findings.claim: Research access to electronic patient record data starts in 2027, and discharge reports, lab results and images must be exchangeable across the EU from March 2031.
findings.detail: ePA: transfer procedure from October 2026, staged technical transfer from mid-December, research use in 2027 (Health Ministry FAQ, https://www.bundesgesundheitsministerium.de/themen/gesundheitswesen/forschungsdatenzentrum-fdz-gesundheit-fragen-und-antworten). EHDS: in force since 26 March 2025; first categories and most secondary use from March 2029.
findings.source: European Commission, EHDS Regulation; Federal Ministry of Health, FAQ FDZ Gesundheit
findings.talk_use: Timeline slide: structured documents become a legal duty.

caveats: FDPG figures differ by source for the same month: 27 million persons (slide) vs 21 million (TMF report); 550,000 consents vs 450,000 (heise).
RACOON site counts vary: 36 (2021), 38 (2025), 39 (Nov 2026); staff nearly 400 vs about 600.
MeDIC Münster pages are undated; confirm the PDF limit and application route before presenting.
'Runs locally' does not mean 'may process patient data'; Bonn needed sign-off from management, compliance, data protection and information security.
RACOON stack is only partly open source: Kaapana is open, mint Lesion and ImFusion come from commercial companies.
FDPG counts show availability, not data already delivered.
Several key results are preprints (Bonn, archive structuring) or were read only as abstracts.
Most web pages were read through a summarising fetch tool; quotes on MeDIC, UniGPT and HHU pages were checked against raw text.
gaps: Search budget ran out before Erlangen, Freiburg and Charité figures, cancer registries and KISSKI details were found.
No public source on RACOON-RAVEN, on SHIP-AI within RACOON, or on RACOON-BASE.
No public source on Münster's RACOON funding share or node leadership; a UKM patient sheet naming RACOON-COMBINE returns 404 (snippet only).
No public UKM AI strategy or UKM-internal LLM (UKMGPT) found.
University of Münster confidentiality class for patient data is in an internal handbook.
ISiK certification status of ORBIS not verified; no survey on FHIR, openEHR and OMOP adoption in German hospitals found.
Status of the Medizinregistergesetz after 27 October 2026 unknown.
